Tempered growth and spectral cutoffs

Reconstructed and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Earlier edition: GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Original exposition: CC0. Supplied foundations retain their stated licences.

Rapid oscillation can make a smooth function with exponential amplitude tempered. The decisive comparison below is between the amplitude and the scale on which the phase changes. A separate global statement characterizes compact Fourier support by an exact Schwartz-convolution identity. Finally, escaping positive masses show that local order zero need not give a small Fourier order, even on one fixed ball.

All pairings are complex linear, without conjugation. The complete Schwartz and Fourier foundation, F1–F5, proves the test space, cutoff density, every Fourier seminorm estimate, both inversion identities, the exact Gaussian transform and all transposed differential identities. We use the equivalent increasing seminorms Their equivalence follows from and the monomial-weight comparison proved in F1. Thus a tempered functional satisfies for some . The proof is the finite-neighborhood rescaling argument in F5. It restricts to a distribution on compact tests by U008, Proposition 1.2.

A family is bounded when every is uniformly bounded on it. Weak convergence in means convergence on each test; the strong dual seminorms are for these bounded families. Our Fourier convention is F1–F5 proves on both spaces and the compatibility with ordinary integrable functions.

The scalar foundations, §§12, 13.1–13.5 and 13.7–13.10, supply completeness, compactness, FTC, exponential and trigonometric identities and cutoffs. The integration foundations, §§15.0–15.2 and 16, supply the absolute and dominated integrations used here. U021, B0–B2 and Theorems 1.1–2.1, supplies compact-test localization and convolution. The exact finite-jet theorem used in Solution 5 is proved in the angular foundations, A2–A3.

Two elementary weighted facts will be used repeatedly: For the first, square both sides and use For the second, the unit ball is contained in a finite cube. On each shell , , the integrand is at most and the shell lies in a cube of volume . The integral is bounded by a constant times . In particular a smooth function bounded by defines a tempered distribution, with a bound by .

The cutoff must be one on a neighborhood of the spectral support; matching a value at a point need not preserve derivatives of a point mass. Solution 4 checks the exact derivative correction.

A measure whose Fourier order is large on a small ball

Theorem 4.1 (escaping masses). Let be unbounded and any integer. There is a tempered distribution supported in , of local order zero, whose Fourier transform has order greater than in the unit ball.

Proof. Set . Inductively choose with and , using unboundedness at each step. The points escape every compact set, hence form a closed locally finite set: a convergent sequence among them must eventually lie in a compact ball, which contains only finitely many points. Define On a compact test only finitely many positive masses occur, so its pairing is bounded by a constant times the test supremum. On Schwartz tests the sum converges absolutely, since This is a tempered distribution of local order zero. Every chosen point is detected by a bump supported away from the other points, so its exact support is the selected set, contained in . The set itself need not be closed.

Choose real nonnegative with , and set . Ordinary differentiation and compact support give a smooth test supported in a compact subset of . It contradicts (4.3), because and . If , (4.3) shows that the restriction is nonzero; its ordinary distributional order is nonnegative, hence greater than .
